entries.title: Galápagos Islands
entries.answer: The Galápagos Islands lie far west of Ecuador’s mainland in the Pacific. Eruptions built the islands from the seafloor, so they were separated from the continent from the start. Plants and animals arrived over water in different ways, and their descendants changed over many generations. Some became different from living things elsewhere. Charles Darwin’s visit helped him think about how animals on separate islands can develop different shapes and habits.
facts: Giant tortoises and land iguanas live on the islands.
Ocean currents from different directions meet around the Galápagos.

entries.title: Grand Canyon
entries.answer: The Grand Canyon is a huge cut through rock in northern Arizona. Far below its rim, the Colorado River has been lifting and carrying away pieces of rock for millions of years. Rain and rockslides help widen the sides as the river keeps cutting. The canyon walls show stripes of different rocks. Some rock near the bottom is much older than the canyon itself, because it was already there when the river began cutting down.
facts: Parts of the canyon are over a mile deep.
Some rocks seen near the bottom formed more than a billion years ago.

entries.title: Great Barrier Reef
entries.answer: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Australia’s northeastern coast. It is made of thousands of separate reefs rather than one long unbroken wall. Small coral animals build hard skeletons, and over time new generations grow onto the old structures. The reefs leave hiding places and feeding spots for many animals. On a map some parts of the system meet open ocean, while others protect shallower stretches of sea closer to the shore.
facts: The Great Barrier Reef runs for about 2,300 kilometers along the northeastern side of Australia.

entries.title: Lake Baikal
entries.answer: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world. Looking at the thin shape it makes on a map gives little hint of how much water is below the surface. The deep opening formed as large areas of rock moved apart. Baikal has fresh water and is home to some animals that live nowhere else, including a seal that spends its life far from any ocean.
facts: At its deepest, Lake Baikal is roughly a mile deep.
Lake Baikal contains a huge share of the fresh water found in the world’s lakes.

entries.title: Mount Kilimanjaro
entries.answer: Mount Kilimanjaro rises from the plains of northern Tanzania to the highest point in Africa. It is made of several volcanoes joined together. A climber passes through different environments, from wooded mountain slopes into cold, mostly bare country near the top. That change happens in a surprisingly short distance because the trail climbs so high. Near the equator the lowlands can be warm while the summit is cold enough for ice.
facts: Kilimanjaro’s highest point is nearly 5,900 meters above sea level.

entries.title: Victoria Falls
entries.answer: The Zambezi River spreads wide at the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, then suddenly pours into a deep, narrow crack in the rock. The water hits with enough force to throw fine drops high above the cliffs. Wind blows this mist onto nearby land, watering plants even when rain has not fallen there. The volume of water changes with the season, so the falls do not always look exactly the same.
facts: Mosi-oa-Tunya is one of the local names for the falls, often translated as “the smoke that thunders.”
